title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution completed all planned pairs (complete_pairs = 200) consuming 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). A randomized 10% Mininet holdout (20 tasks) produced zero validator–emulator disagreements per the archived contamination summary; however the explicit randomized selection seed for that holdout is not present in the labeled artifacts, preventing bit‑for‑bit reconstruction of the drawn holdout. Because baseline validator failures were absent, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We report the sealed design, precise execution accounting, artifact‑grounded diagnostics, and an evidence‑based discussion of operational implications and threats to validity (preregistration id: cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02).

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with generative language models can improve NetOps productivity but risks generating incorrect or unsafe changes that cause outages or policy violations. Prior work therefore proposes grounding, deterministic validation, and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR) to detect and correct unsafe candidates prior to application. The operational value of automated repair depends on (i) baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures under the chosen generator/prompting policy, (ii) validator coverage and fidelity, and (iii) repair budget and repair‑prompt effectiveness. We preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory question and paired design to isolate the marginal effect of invoking a deterministic validator and a single automated repair attempt on the identical generator output: Does an automated, deterministic GVR pipeline materially reduce validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank?
sections.related_work: Empirical studies and surveys document LLM factual errors, prompt sensitivity, non‑determinism, and mitigation approaches such as retrieval grounding, verifier‑assisted repair, and guarded agent architectures. NetOps prototype systems show feasibility of intent→configuration generation but typically stop short of instrumented, production‑like failure‑rate evaluations. Architectural proposals recommend combining LLM generation with deterministic validators (Batfish‑style checkers) and using secondary emulation or testbeds to expose validator blind spots. Red‑team audits and configuration‑brittleness studies show that tool descriptions, persona/history, and tool‑chaining can materially change safety outcomes. This work situates itself as a preregistered, artifact‑grounded measurement that isolates the incremental effect of deterministic repair for a fixed model and sampling policy, complementing prior prototype and threat analyses.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design. The preregistered plan (cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02) fixed a paired design with n = 200 tasks, one shared deterministic initial generation per task, and a repair budget of at most one automated repair call per task. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline and the primary test an exact two‑sided McNemar test (α = 0.05). Bootstrap percentile 95% CIs used 10,000 resamples with bootstrap_seed = 1729.

Task bank and validators. The confirmatory sample is a curated machine‑checkable intent→configuration bank (200 tasks across four topology clusters: enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge; 50 tasks each). Tasks encode initial/final states and workflow constraints (make_before_break, must_be_down_for_fields, group minima). The primary deterministic checker (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforces syntactic and intent/constraint checks and emits structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). A Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator was preregistered as a secondary disagreement detector applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to detect validator–emulator mismatches; the post‑run contamination summary reports zero disagreements for that holdout (see archived contamination artifact described below). We note and discuss below an explicit reproducibility limitation: the labeled artifacts do not include the randomized selection seed used to draw the Mininet 10% holdout, which prevents exact reconstruction of that specific holdout selection.

Adapter semantics and enforced determinism. The hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter enforced shared_initial generation semantics: a single initial generator invocation per task was produced and reused for both baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (GVR) conditions. The canonical execution accounting from the archived run documents model_calls_used = 200, hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 0, and stage_counts showing shared_initial_generation = 200. These audited fields demonstrate that determinism was achieved by adapter enforcement (single shared initial invocation per task) rather than by relying solely on a listed model parameter. Note: execution/model_configuration.json lists the model selection as gpt‑5‑mini and the model parameter "temperature": null; the runtime determinism in this run was produced by the adapter’s shared_initial semantics and is auditable via the deterministic reconciliation/provider‑call audit artifacts enumerated below.

Execution contract, repair policy, and stopping. The execution contract limited model calls to a maximum of 400 (200 initial + up to 200 repairs); adapter enforcement resulted in 200 model calls used (one shared initial generation per task) and repair_calls_used = 0. The preregistered repair policy allowed at most one automated repair prompt to the same LLM when the primary validator reported violations; any repaired candidate would be re‑validated. Missingness/exclusion rules deterministically excluded pairs where both conditions failed due to infrastructure execution failures; tasks flagged for validator–emulator disagreement would be excluded from the primary analysis per the contamination plan, with sensitivity analyses preregistered for alternative treatments.

Statistical procedures. The primary test is the exact McNemar two‑sided test on the paired 2×2 table (n11, n10, n01, n00). Confidence intervals used the paired bootstrap percentile method with 10,000 resamples (seed = 1729). Secondary exploratory analyses (planned) include logistic regressions and descriptive summaries for repair iteration counts and model‑call costs; these are executed only when applicable data are present.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and adapter audit. The autonomous run processed all planned episodes: completed_episode_count = 400 (shared initial generation reused across baseline and guarded conditions), complete_pair_count = 200, model_calls_used = 200, maximum_model_calls = 400, repair_calls_used = 0. Provider/audit artifacts recorded hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 0, cache_miss_count = 200, and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}, confirming single shared invocations per task and adapter enforcement of determinism.

Validator outcomes and primary contingency. Every shared initial candidate passed the primary deterministic validator: baseline_success_count = 200/200 and guarded_success_count = 200/200. The paired contingency table is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Observed paired difference estimate = 0.0. The prespecified exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Because baseline validator failures were absent, the preregistered confirmatory hypothesis (≥50% relative reduction) could not be meaningfully evaluated on this sample under the preregistered estimand.

Contamination check. The preregistered Mininet emulator was executed on a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) as a secondary disagreement detector; the analysis/contamination_summary artifact reports zero validator–emulator disagreement flags for that holdout. We emphasize the reproducibility limitation that the explicit randomized selection seed that determined which tasks comprised the 10% Mininet holdout is not present among the labeled artifacts, which prevents exact deterministic reconstruction of the holdout draw even though the contamination summary records zero disagreements.

Repair and secondary outcomes. No validator failures occurred; consequently the preregistered repair branch was never triggered and no repair artifacts or repair‑iteration statistics were produced. Preplanned secondary estimands (average repair iterations per repaired task, GVR‑introduced failure rate, model‑call cost per successful repair) are therefore empty for this run and are recorded as such in the archived analysis outputs.

Representative diagnostics. Representative validator traces in the archived bundle show parsed_command_count matching required_command_count and validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true for sampled tasks; task difficulty annotations include levels labeled "medium", "hard", and "very_hard" with dependency patterns such as make_before_break_uplink_switchover and paired_link_atomic_mtu_change, indicating the task bank exercised nontrivial dependency constraints despite all outputs satisfying the deterministic checks under the chosen generation policy.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation. The null outcome (zero baseline validator failures) is an artifact‑grounded empirical result: under the sealed paired design and adapter‑enforced shared_initial semantics, there were no validator‑detectable failures for the GVR pipeline to reduce. The exact McNemar p = 1.0 and bootstrap CI = [0.0, 0.0] precisely reflect that degeneracy. These numbers do not imply that repair is universally unnecessary: the marginal value of automated repair depends on baseline failure prevalence and validator coverage for the targeted workload and generation policy.

Why the null occurred. Archived diagnostics suggest three contributing factors: (1) the generator/prompt policy used here produced candidates that satisfied the machine‑checkable constraints embedded in the task bank (parsed_command_count matched required_command_count across tasks); (2) the task bank, while including tasks labeled with nontrivial dependency patterns, is a curated set whose constructs the generator matched under the used prompt and model; (3) the paired shared_initial design intentionally removed sampling variance between conditions and therefore did not allow the primary contrast to capture benefits obtainable via multi‑sample generation or higher sampling temperature.

Methodological tradeoffs and implications. The shared_initial paired design isolates the causal effect of invoking validation+repair on the identical generator output; it trades internal control for a narrower external question. Evaluators seeking unconditional operational failure rates should adopt independent per‑condition multi‑sample draws (or ensembles) to estimate unconditional failure prevalence and to expose repair opportunities hidden by single‑draw designs. Practitioners should measure baseline validator failure prevalence on representative workloads and probe validator coverage (via emulation, testbeds, and adversarial perturbations) before allocating significant engineering effort to automated repair when baseline failures are already rare.

Validator coverage and reproducibility caveat. Deterministic validators are necessary but not sufficient oracles: they codify a specific set of checks; end‑to‑end emulation or device tests can reveal blind spots. The Mininet holdout produced zero disagreements in the sampled 20 tasks, but the absent labeled selection seed limits bit‑for‑bit reproducibility of that exact draw; this omission is a documented reproducibility gap that constrains the strength of conclusions about validator completeness drawn from that holdout.

Recommendations for future confirmatory studies. To measure GVR effectiveness where baseline failure prevalence is low, preregistered runs should (i) include independent per‑condition multi‑sample draws and multi‑model comparisons to estimate unconditional failure prevalence; (ii) increase repair budgets and allow multi‑step or human‑escalated repairs; (iii) scale secondary emulation checks and record selection seeds to enable exact reproduction of holdout draws; (iv) expand validator fidelity with richer device models or vendor‑specific semantics; and (v) include adversarial perturbation/red‑team evaluations to probe configuration brittleness.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs), yielding an observed paired difference of 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, and bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Because baseline validator failures were absent, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated. The artifact‑grounded outcome highlights that GVR’s measured marginal value is workload and validator dependent; when baseline validator‑detectable failures are rare under the intended generation policy, a single‑pass automated repair budget yields no measured benefit for those validator‑detected errors. We archive all execution and analysis outputs for independent inspection and recommend follow‑up confirmatory designs that target workloads with nontrivial baseline failure prevalence, larger repair budgets, broader emulator/testbed coverage, and multi‑sample/multi‑model policies.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (mandatory). This study executed under the autonomous post‑lock preregistration cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02. The exact initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Topic constraints: the human Research Director limited the study to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focusing on safety/reliability of generated network changes. Frameworks and tools: orchestration used hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and the deterministic task generator deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Primary deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (intent/constraint checks). A Mininet‑based emulator was preregistered and executed as a secondary disagreement detector on a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks); the archived contamination summary reports zero disagreements for that holdout but the explicit randomized selection seed for the holdout is not present among the labeled artifacts (documented reproducibility gap). Preregistration and freeze: the experimental plan (estimand, sample size n = 200, paired design, stopping rules, max model calls = 400, repair budget = 1 per task, shared‑initial generation semantics) was frozen before any model calls. Autonomous execution and artifacts: the run executed autonomously under the frozen plan (start: 2026‑08‑30T11:50:34.530059Z; end: 2026‑08‑30T12:12:07.541650Z); audited execution accounting recorded model_calls_used = 200 and repair_calls_used = 0. Determinism note: execution/model_configuration.json lists "temperature": null; runtime determinism in this run was produced by the adapter’s shared_initial_generation enforcement (audited fields include hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts showing shared_initial_generation = 200, as recorded in the deterministic reconciliation/provider‑call audit artifacts). Human involvement: the human Research Director selected the topic family and pre‑lock constraints; no human manual editing or selective rewriting of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. Deviations and restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred. The archived execution bundle contains canonical artifacts that substantiate the claims in the paper (examples: execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/model_configuration.json, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/contamination_summary.csv, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl, deterministic_reconciliation.json).
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested (audited hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts shared_initial_generation = 200). Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.
